stem:
A 21-day-old term boy has a temperature of 38.4 °C measured at home and confirmed in the emergency department. He is feeding a little less than usual but is alert, pink and well perfused, with a heart rate of 170/min. There is no focal source on examination. A catheter urine dipstick is positive for leucocytes and nitrites.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Urine culture and oral cefalexin, with review in 24 hours
options.explanation: A febrile neonate is not managed with oral antibiotics at home, even when the dipstick suggests a urinary source.

options.label: B
options.text: Blood, urine and CSF cultures, then IV antibiotics
options.explanation: Correct. A febrile infant under 28 days needs a full sepsis evaluation including LP and prompt empirical IV antibiotics, however well he looks and whatever the urine shows.

options.label: C
options.text: Admit for observation and urine culture, without antibiotics
options.explanation: Observation without antibiotics is unsafe in a febrile neonate, as bacterial infection can progress quickly despite a well appearance.

options.label: D
options.text: FBC and CRP, with IV antibiotics only if either is raised
options.explanation: Normal inflammatory markers do not exclude serious bacterial infection in a neonate, so they cannot decide who receives antibiotics.

options.label: E
options.text: Blood and urine cultures and IV antibiotics; LP not needed
options.explanation: A positive dipstick does not exclude coexisting bacteraemia or meningitis in the first month, so neonates need CSF sampling as part of the sepsis work-up.

context: A febrile infant under 28 days needs blood, urine and CSF cultures and empirical IV antibiotics, even if well-appearing and even when the urine explains the fever.
